summary:
Equilibria is a browser game that turns young learners into cadets on a Moon base at the lunar south pole. A signal from the Moon calls them, and an AI guide, LUNIA, (EN: Lunar Utilization of Natural resources by Intelligent Agents; ES: Logística y Uso de recursos Naturales con Inteligencia Artificial) welcomes them aboard. Before launch, a short skills test uses Bartle’s player types (Achievers, Explorers, Socializers) to discover each child’s learning style, and the game adapts to it. Cadets then design their own astronaut avatar, which stays with them through every mission.

Along the way they face the real trade-offs of living in space: oxygen, energy, radiation shielding and limited budgets. Explorers unlock real NASA data cards, such as DONKI space-weather readings and OSDR findings, and can experiment in a lab mode. Achievers earn stars and badges, and Socializers build a crew with its own personality.

Everything runs with cinematic 3D scenes and a sci-fi soundscape, with no install needed. Equilibria matters because it makes NASA science personal: every child learns that surviving beyond Earth is about balance, and that they can be part of it. Tha's where its name comes from: equilibria, the balance that holds life together.
details:
Mission Equilibria: keep the Moon alive. Keep her company.

A signal comes in from the Moon’s south pole. It’s faint. It’s scared. And it needs you.

Meet LUNIA, the AI that runs a lunar outpost. She’s brilliant, she’s fragile, and she’s afraid of being switched off and left alone. You are the cadet who answers the call. Your mission: keep the base alive for the astronauts coming next, and keep LUNIA from fading out.

Every kid plays their own game. Before launch, a ten-challenge profile test reads how each child plays, using Bartle’s player types and traits like persistence, risk and pace. The child only sees their specialty: Achiever, Explorer or Socializer. Behind the scenes, the game tunes difficulty and support to keep them in that sweet spot: never bored, never lost. Then they build their own astronaut, and that avatar stays with them to the end.

Then comes the launch. Fire the engine at exactly the right moment, or fly right past the Moon. Miss? Try again, as often as you like. Nobody explains orbital windows. You feel them.

Then five missions, your choice of order: life support, radiation shielding, energy, food and communication delay. Every choice has a price. Shield the base from a solar storm and tonight’s power drops. Research more and the oxygen runs thin. No option is free. That’s the whole lesson of deep space, learned by deciding, not by reading.

And while you work, something quiet happens. As each mission is completed, LUNIA grows brighter and warmer, with a new color in her light and a new expression on her face. Kids don’t just finish missions. They protect someone.

Missions are designed around real NASA sources, including DONKI solar activity and OSDR astronaut health data, so kids know they are touching real science. Failure is safe, there is no ranking, and it runs in any browser with no downloads or accounts, from a classroom to a kitchen table. Built with Three.js, Canvas, Web Audio and Tone.js, it has cinematic 3D scenes and a sci-fi soundtrack that reacts to every key press and screen change.

Why it matters: children walk away knowing one true thing about space: every resource is limited, and every decision moves the cost somewhere else. They practice systems thinking and decisions under constraints, and many of them, especially Latin American kids who rarely see themselves in space stories, may see that they belong up there too.

Finish all five missions and a rocket to Mars awaits, where the same trade-offs return, harder.
